result.summary: Pausanias finishes the Delphi statues with the diver Scyllis and his daughter Hydna, then tells how Methymna's fishermen found an olive-wood head of Dionysus. He describes the temple gables and golden arms, and begins his account of the Gallic (Galati) invasions of Greece under Cambaules and Brennus.

scenes.title: Scyllis and Hydna the divers
scenes.summary: Statues of the diver Scyllis and his daughter Hydna stand at Delphi. They cut Xerxes' ships' cables in a storm, and Nero later took Hydna's statue.

scenes.title: The olive-wood head of Dionysus
scenes.summary: Methymna fishermen net an olive-wood head. The Pythian priestess tells them to worship Phallenian Dionysus, and they send a bronze copy to Delphi.
scenes.stakes: The Methymnians need to know which god the strange image represents.

scenes.title: Gables and golden arms
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the temple gables, their sculptors, and the shields offered on the architraves.

scenes.title: The Gallic expeditions begin
scenes.summary: After Cambaules' first raid, a larger Celtic army splits in three. Bolgius defeats and kills Ptolemy of Macedon, but the Celts withdraw.
scenes.stakes: Macedonia and Thrace face invasion and plunder.

scenes.title: Brennus musters the great army
scenes.summary: Brennus persuades the Galati to invade Greece for its wealth. Pausanias describes their huge army and the Trimarcisia cavalry system.
scenes.stakes: Greece and its rich temples face invasion.

alias_notes.explanation: Pausanias uses Galati and Celts for the same people.

notable_quotes.reason: Gives the Celtic word marca for horse, explaining the name Trimarcisia.

analysis.text: Pausanias mixes dedications and sculptors with history, showing how Delphi's offerings record Greek memory, including war against outsiders.
The Gallic invasion of 279 BC and its attack on Delphi became a defining Greek memory of resisting barbarians.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias' figures for the Gallic army are probably greatly exaggerated.

language_notes.text: Amphictyones were the member states of the Amphictyonic League, which administered Delphi; here they dedicate the statue as a collective offering.
A bracketed line, apparently a later insertion or editor's aside, about divers; its sense is obscure and it is not clearly Pausanias' own.
"Fished up" means dragged up in the nets; the head was an unexpected catch, not a made offering.
Phallenian is an epithet of Dionysus, linked to the phallus; Pausanias gives no explanation here.
Architraves are the main beams resting on the columns; the shields were fixed along them.
Galati are the Gauls (Celts), who invaded Greece and attacked Delphi in 279 BC; the Ætolians fought them.
Refers to Pausanias' earlier account in Book 1, tied to the Athenian council-chamber (Metroon/bouleuterion), where he first mentioned the Galatian invasion.
"Egged on" means urged or incited; "enamoured of the gains of looting" means passionately fond of plunder.
"Suppliant" is someone seeking protection; killing one was a grave breach of religious and hospitality norms.
"Durst" is archaic for "dared"; "adventure" here means venture or risk going.
The Immortals were the elite Persian royal infantry, kept always at 10,000 men by replacing any who fell.
Trimarcisia means roughly "three horses" (tri- plus marca); related to the Celtic word for horse.

context_notes.text: Xerxes, king of Persia, invaded Greece in 480 BC; his fleet suffered storms off Mount Pelion in Thessaly before the sea battles.
The Roman emperor Nero removed hundreds of statues from Delphi to adorn Rome, as Pausanias notes elsewhere.
The Pythian priestess was the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, consulted by cities and individuals on religious questions.
Thyiades were frenzied female followers of Dionysus who held rites on Parnassus near Delphi.
The Athenians' victory over the Persians at Marathon came in 490 BC.
Brennus is the main Gallic leader of the invasion; the Triballi and Pæonians were peoples north of Macedonia and Greece.
Ptolemy Ceraunus, exiled son of Ptolemy I of Egypt, seized Macedonia; he died fighting the Gauls in 279 BC. Ceraunus means "Thunderbolt."
Ancient authors often gave very large army figures; Pausanias' numbers should be treated cautiously.

literary_notes.text: The diver pair are honored for a heroic though morally ambiguous act, showing Pausanias' interest in famous individuals who served Greece.
A foreign-looking god is hauled from the sea by ordinary fishermen, and he becomes an honored Greek cult figure.
Ptolemy's treachery toward a suppliant and his nickname paint him as bold and impious, preparing for his downfall.
Brennus appears as a cunning persuader who exploits Greek wealth and weakness, marking him as the driving force.
The closing line, stressing force and intentions, signals the coming clash at Delphi that the chapter promised.
